facts.claim: As of October 2026, the latest Model Context Protocol specification is version 2026-07-28.
MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, responses and notifications.
Hosts are the AI applications, clients are connectors inside a host, and servers provide context and capabilities.
Servers offer three features: tools (functions for the model to run), resources (context and data) and prompts (templated messages for users).
Since version 2026-07-28 MCP keeps no session: there is no opening exchange, and every request carries its own protocol version and what its client supports.
A client may call server/discover to learn a server's supported versions before other requests.
Clients list a server's tools with tools/list and run one with tools/call.
A tool that fails on bad input returns a normal result marked isError, so the model can read the message and try again.
The specification says there should always be a person in the loop who can deny any tool call.
Clients must treat a tool’s annotations, labels such as read-only, as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.

In Zhan et al.’s test (2024) of 1,054 cases, GPT-4, prompted to use tools step by step, followed instructions planted in tool results 24% of the time, and nearly twice as often when the planted text also pushed it to obey.

MCP’s sign-in rules (its authorization framework) cover servers reached over HTTP; a local server connected through standard input and output (stdio) takes its keys and passwords from its environment instead.
The model only returns a structured request to call a tool; the application runs it and sends the result back.
When the model calls a function, the application must execute it and return the result.
A tool is defined by a name, a description of when to use it, and a JSON Schema for its arguments.
Anthropic’s tool-use docs (checked 2026-10-30) call a detailed description, saying what the tool does and when to use it, by far the most important factor in how well Claude uses a tool.
Anthropic and OpenAI both offer a strict mode that makes the model’s tool calls reliably match the tool’s schema.
Models can ask for several tool calls in one turn; Anthropic and OpenAI both let the application limit this to one call per turn.
By default the model decides whether to call a tool; the application can require a call, force a specific tool, or forbid tools.
OpenAI’s Agents SDK, its toolkit for building assistants that use tools, stops a request after 10 turns by default (a turn is one model reply and the calls in it) unless the app sets its own limit.
